title: Hiring manager, senior TPM, average answers

questions.text: Tell me about the most complex program you have run.
How do you handle a project that is slipping?
How do you work with engineering leads who do not report to you?
How do you decide what to escalate?
How have you helped other program managers grow?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Felix, thanks for joining. I'm Sunita, I manage the program management team. This is a thirty minute conversation about your background and the role.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Sunita, thank you for the time.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Did you travel for work this week?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Not this week. I was in the office, so a normal week for once.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Good. I'll ask about a few programs and how you work with others, and we will leave time for your questions.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about the most complex program you have run.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: At Corvane Health I ran a program to move our claims systems to a new vendor. It touched six teams and went on for about a year. We had a plan with milestones and I ran the weekly status meeting. We ended up launching about a month late because of a data migration issue, but the vendor switch itself went fine.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What did you do about the data migration issue?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We found the issue in testing, and I pulled the data team and the vendor into daily calls. I made the call to delay the launch by a month instead of launching with bad records. Leadership was not happy but agreed. After that we added a data check to every milestone.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you handle a project that is slipping?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I try to find the cause early and talk to the team about it. Usually it is a dependency or unclear scope. Then we adjust the plan and tell the stakeholders so there are no surprises. Communication is the key thing.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why this role?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I have run programs for about nine years and I want to work at a larger scale. Your team supports several products, which would stretch me. I also like that the role is close to engineering.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What does a larger scale mean to you?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: More teams and more risk. Right now I run programs with about six teams, and I would like to coordinate fifteen or more. I have not done that yet, so I know there is a gap, but I have mentored two junior program managers and I think I can grow into it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you work with engineering leads who do not report to you?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I try to understand what each lead cares about. For the claims program, one lead was worried about on-call load, so I offered to move two of our tasks to a quieter month. We built trust that way, and she became one of the main supporters. I also keep a shared tracker so nobody gets surprised.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: How are programs handed off between TPMs when someone leaves?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Each program has a written brief and a named backup. A handoff takes two weeks, and the new owner meets every lead in that time.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That is all the time we have. Thanks Felix, the recruiter will contact you next week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Sunita. I enjoyed it.

notes: Average for senior: scope looks mid level. The slipping-project answer is vague and the interviewer moves on without a probe.
